sources.title: Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations
sources.publisher: Springer, on behalf of the European Journal of Epidemiology
sources.version: European Journal of Epidemiology 2016;31(4):337-350; full text as archived in PubMed Central, retrieved 2026-07-25. DOI 10.1007/s10654-016-0149-3, PMID 27209009, PMCID PMC4877414
sources.locator: The section defining the significance level, power, and the beta error rate; and numbered misinterpretations 4, 5, 6 and 24 together with the passage on power computed from observed data and the passages on analysis selection and selective reporting
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License, as stated on the article page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts it states: that the cut-off value alpha is supposed to be fixed in advance and is part of the study design, unchanged in light of the data; that the terms significance level and alpha level refer to that cut-off; that the power of a test to detect a correct alternative hypothesis is the pre-study probability that the test will reject the test hypothesis; that the corresponding pre-study probability of failing to reject the test hypothesis when the alternative is correct is one minus the power and is known as the Type-II or beta error rate; that observing a null-hypothesis P value above 0.05 means only that the null is one among many hypotheses compatible with the data and does not mean that no effect was observed; that a large P value is not evidence in favour of the test hypothesis; that accepting a false null hypothesis leaves the chance of being in error at 100% and not at one minus the power; that power calculated from the observed data is a transformation of the null P value and so provides no test of the alternatives; and that P values are interpretable only if the analyses were not guided toward, or selected for presentation on the basis of, their significance or nonsignificance. No sentence, table, figure, worked example, or numbered item from the article is reproduced or adapted, and the article's CC BY licence is not relied on because nothing from it is reused. The cohort, the two-by-two table, the forty-person study, the journal club, and all wording in this lesson are original.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, section 7.1.3: What are statistical tests?
creators: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology, U.S. Department of Commerce
sources.version: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, online edition retrieved 2026-07-25; no publication or revision date is stated on the page
sources.locator: Section 7.1.3, What are statistical tests?, under the headings on errors of the first and second kind and the significance level
sources.license: US Government work; NIST states that information on its sites is public information and may be distributed or copied, with credit requested

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts the page states: that the risk of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is in fact true is denoted alpha and is often referred to as the significance level of the test; that the risk of failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is in fact false is denoted beta and is usually referred to as the error of the second kind; that beta is not chosen by the user but depends on the size of the actual discrepancy, so that large discrepancies are easier to detect and lead to small errors of the second kind while small discrepancies lead to large ones; that the risk beta increases as the risk alpha decreases; and that the risks of errors of the second kind are usually summarised by an operating characteristic curve. No wording, table, figure, or example from the handbook is reproduced or adapted; the two-by-two decision table in this lesson was constructed here and the page carries no such table. NIST copyright guidance at https://www.nist.gov/oism/copyrights states that NIST information is public information that may be distributed or copied and requests appropriate credit.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, section 7.2.2.2: Sample sizes required
creators: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology, U.S. Department of Commerce
sources.version: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, online edition retrieved 2026-07-25; no publication or revision date is stated on the page
sources.locator: Section 7.2.2.2, Sample sizes required, covering the inputs to a sample-size calculation and the formulas for the one-sided and two-sided cases with the standard deviation known
sources.license: US Government work; NIST states that information on its sites is public information and may be distributed or copied, with credit requested

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts the page states: that a sample size is chosen from the risk alpha of rejecting a true hypothesis, the risk beta of accepting a false null hypothesis when a particular value of the alternative is true, the standard deviation of the measurement, and the size of the difference that is meaningful to detect; and that for a two-sided test with the standard deviation known the required sample size is the square of the sum of the two normal quantiles for alpha and beta, multiplied by the square of the ratio of the standard deviation to that difference. No wording, table, figure, or worked example from the handbook is reproduced or adapted; the handbook's own worked example is a one-sided single-sample case at beta 0.10 and is not used, and every sample size in this lesson is a two-group calculation performed here from the block's own figures. NIST copyright guidance at https://www.nist.gov/oism/copyrights states that NIST information is public information that may be distributed or copied and requests appropriate credit.

sources.title: A general introduction to adjustment for multiple comparisons
sources.publisher: AME Publishing Company, for the Journal of Thoracic Disease
sources.version: Journal of Thoracic Disease 2017;9(6):1725-1729; full text as archived in PubMed Central, retrieved 2026-07-25. DOI 10.21037/jtd.2017.05.34, PMID 28740688, PMCID PMC5506159
sources.locator: The passages defining the Type I error and the family-wise error rate, the illustration of error inflation across large numbers of simultaneously tested true hypotheses, and the description of the Bonferroni correction
sources.license: Copyright 2017 Journal of Thoracic Disease, all rights reserved, as printed on the article page; free full text via PubMed Central. No open reuse licence stated, so this pack uses facts only.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts it states: that a Type I error is the incorrect rejection of a true null hypothesis; that the family-wise error rate is the probability of incorrectly rejecting at least one true null hypothesis; that testing many hypotheses simultaneously makes at least one incorrect rejection close to inevitable, with the article's own illustrations at 100 and at 10,000 independent true hypotheses tested at a significance level of 0.05; and that the Bonferroni correction adjusts the threshold to the significance level divided by the number of tests and is conservative when that number is large. No sentence, table, figure, p-value set, or worked example from the article is reproduced or adapted; the article's six-hypothesis illustration is not used, and every multiplicity figure in this lesson was computed here from the block's own study. The arithmetic 1 minus 0.95 raised to the power k is derived in the lesson from the complement rule and independence, which an earlier lesson in this block establishes, and is not taken from this source.

sources.title: Subgroup analyses in confirmatory clinical trials: time to be specific about their purposes
sources.publisher: BioMed Central, for BMC Medical Research Methodology
sources.version: BMC Medical Research Methodology 2016;16:20; full text as archived in PubMed Central, retrieved 2026-07-25. DOI 10.1186/s12874-016-0122-6, PMID 26891992, PMCID PMC4757983
sources.locator: The passages on the statistical and methodological issues affecting subgroup analyses, including inflation of type I error due to multiple testing, the distinction between prespecified and post hoc analyses, and the standing of subgroup analyses as exploratory
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License, as stated on the article page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts it states: that subgroup analyses are prone to statistical and methodological issues including inflation of type I error due to multiple testing; that reports frequently fail to make clear whether a subgroup analysis was prespecified or performed post hoc, and that this distinction governs how the result may be read; and that subgroup analyses are exploratory because their level of evidence is too weak to reach a definite answer, with replication in an independent trial the recommended route. No sentence, table, figure, or example from the article is reproduced or adapted, and the article's CC BY licence is not relied on because nothing from it is reused. The twenty-subgroup case, its arithmetic, and the three candidate report sentences in this lesson are original.
